body:
> This is likely just from "alphabetical" sorting, where `_` just has a higher score than any other character

No, this behavior is the one intended by the current sorting algorithm, which sorts by scope and then alphabetical. Suggestions are first sorted by class hierarchy (because in general you are much more likely to use stuff from the current class), so print ranks lower because it is in the global scope while print_orphan_nodes is a method on Node.

It's a bit unfortunate for this print case (which I run into ever once in a while as well). But overall the approach works better than whatever we did in 3.x IMO.

We also can't rank the global scope higher, because it would clutter completions with all the unrelated node types that exist.

To fix this, we'd either have to factor in some threshold of alphabetical matching which allows options to get ranked up in the scope sorting. But getting this right is probably impossible.

Maybe we should just hack a list of global scope methods into the algorithm that get lifted to the `Node` scope. We can then curate the few common cases were the algorithm does a very bad job.

> Maybe we should just hack a list of global scope methods into the algorithm that get lifted to the `Node` scope. We can then curate the few common cases were the algorithm does a very bad job.

How about a list of favourite function names in Editor Settings. If a favourite functions is found in the suggestion list, it is raised to the top. For example I pretty much never use `print()`, I always use `prints()`, so `prints()` would be on my favourite list, but `print()` wouldn't.

> which sorts by scope and then alphabetical

of course i don't know how it works exactly and it might already do this, but i feel like it should consider "distance"/String.similarity() and do all of this at the same time, creating an overall score from the three (or more, if type is added) factors instead of doing one after the other.

> How about a list of favourite function names in Editor Settings

this could be neat. or just some way to influence the rankings as a user.  
though at that point one could consider usage-based completions, counting how many times a function was used to prioritise. probably overkill tho
